I am building a new home for my technical writing at [kaushiksinha.com](https://kaushiksinha.com/). I wanted the freedom of a notebook for exploration, but I also wanted the typography and structure of a proper article. That led me to an experiment with [marimo](https://marimo.io/), [marimo Studio](https://github.com/marimo-team/marimo-studio), and [Quarto](https://quarto.org/).

## The idea

The notebook should own the computation, controls, and decisions. A published view should own the presentation.

That separation sounds simple:

1. Author the analysis in a marimo notebook.
2. Create a Studio view from the notebook.
3. Use Quarto to present the view as a polished document.

To test the pipeline, I made a tiny notebook with a slider. The notebook computes the square of the selected number, and the Quarto view displays the result.

## The first obstacle

The Quarto provider was available in the development version of marimo Studio, but installing that development package did not provide the browser assets needed by the Studio server. The editor started, but the browser returned an HTTP 500 because `build-meta.json` was missing.

The fix was to build Studio from its source repository. That required the JavaScript build toolchain in addition to the Python environment. The first build attempt used Node.js 26 and stopped because one of the frontend scripts still passed `--experimental-transform-types`, an option that Node 26 no longer accepts.

Fortunately, the source setup had also installed Node.js 24.19.0 in its Python environment. Running the build with that Node version produced the browser assets successfully.

## A minimal notebook

The smallest useful test is a notebook with one control, one computation, and one displayed result:

```python
import marimo

app = marimo.App()


@app.cell
def _():
    import marimo as mo

    rounds = mo.ui.slider(1, 100, value=10, label="Rounds")
    rounds
    return mo, rounds


@app.cell
def _(rounds):
    total = rounds.value**2
    return (total,)


@app.cell
def _(mo, rounds, total):
    mo.md(f"The square of **{rounds.value}** is **{total}**.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run()
```

Moving the slider to 36 changed the Quarto view to:

> The square of 36 is 1296.

That small example tested the complete path rather than just checking that the editor opened.

## Reproduce this setup

The following is the source-build workflow I used on macOS. It reflects the state of the tools on 17 October 2026; a later Studio release may make some of these steps unnecessary.

First install Pixi with its official installer and make it available in the current shell:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://pixi.sh/install.sh | sh
source ~/.zshrc
```

The frontend build also needs pnpm. With Node.js installed, install the version specified by Studio:

```bash
npm install --global pnpm@11.28.2
```

Clone Studio beside the blog repository and run its setup:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/marimo-team/marimo-studio.git
cd marimo-studio
make setup
```

If the setup reaches the frontend build with Node.js 26 and reports `bad option: --experimental-transform-types`, rerun it with the Node.js 24.19.0 binary that the setup placed in the Python environment:

```bash
PATH="$PWD/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/nodejs_wheel/bin:$PATH" make setup
```

In the blog project, point `marimo-studio` at the pinned preview wheel while the Quarto provider remains unreleased:

```toml
[tool.uv.sources]
marimo-studio = { url = "https://github.com/marimo-team/marimo-studio/releases/download/preview/marimo_studio-0.3.1.dev30-py3-none-any.whl" }
```

Then run `uv sync`, open the notebook with marimo, create a view, and choose **Quarto document**. The wheel includes both the Quarto provider and the browser assets, so another machine does not need a sibling Studio checkout. It is still a preview release, so the dependency should be revisited when a stable package includes the provider.

## What I learned

The difficult part was not Quarto itself. Quarto was already installed and could render the document. The friction came from using an unreleased Studio provider and therefore needing to build Studio's browser assets locally.

The experiment also clarified the boundary between the tools:

- **marimo** owns the notebook and its reactive computation;
- **Studio** connects notebook results to named views;
- **Quarto** supplies the document structure and presentation.

This may become easier as marimo Studio matures. For now, I am treating the setup as an experiment rather than a final installation recipe. The important result is that the architecture works: a control in a marimo notebook can drive a polished Quarto view.

## Next steps

The prototype is now committed in the site repository and uses a pinned, portable Studio preview wheel. I still need to create the site's normal navigation and landing page, and then begin migrating selected posts from the old blog.
